text.p: European Union Commissioner for Agriculture and Rural Development, Franz Fischler, stressed cooperation ahead of meetings with the Australian government on Thursday, sidestepping questions about EC grain subsidies.

But he said the EC did not plan to side with the United States in taking Australia before the World Trade Organisation over the Australian Wheat Board's single desk monopoly on Australian wheat exports.

The main message he would take to meetings with Australian Prime Minister John Howard, Deputy Prime Minister and Trade Minister Tim Fischer and Primary Industries Minister John Anderson would focus on EU agricultural policy reforms and completion of a veterinary agreement with Australia, he said.
Fischler noted that his was the first visit to Australia an EU farm commissioner in 10 years.
He said the main message he wished to impress on Australian authorities was tremendous change in Europe.
But on specifics, an Australia-EC veterinary agreement conclusion was in prospect for later this year, he said.
Much progress had been made in recent months with the agreement now settled on main principles, he said.

Settlement of the issue of European access to Australia for cooked chicken and pork meat was not seen as a precondition for the veterinary agreement, he said. But Fischler later criticised Australia's presently closed door to imported cooked pig meat.
European countries could export pig meat to Japan, which also had high standards.
"It is not understandable for us why some countries which export to Japan cannot export to Australia," he said.
Fischler's optimistic comments on an Australia-EC veterinary agreement follows critical comments earlier this week on the issue by Australian Primary Industries Minister Anderson.

Anderson said Europe had placed real pressure on Australia to agree to regional equivalency under which Australia would be required to take products from one part of Europe if equivalent products were taken from another part.
Australian barriers against imports of cooked pork and chicken meat were another stumbling bloock, Anderson said.
Speaking with reporters on Thursday morning, Fischler defended EU agricultural export subsidies, with grains subsidies flexible and linked with world market prices.
It was not in the EC's interest to "destroy the trade" but to bridge price differentials, he said.
The EU would reduce subsidies if returns from world markets allowed it, he said. Australia and the EU were also selling farm produce into "very different places in the world," he added.
There was clear evidence that the EC did not lower world wheat prices through agricultural subsidies. Accusations by the U.S. that the EC reduced wheat prices were not fair, he said.
Fischler also said Australia and the EC were still pursuing avenues to resolve differences on a framework agreement in which the EC wishes to include a controversial clause on human rights.
"We are still pursuing avenues on both sides to try to get over the current difficulties," he said.
"It is important not to pre-judge the issue. Perhaps even more important is to concentrate on the overall improved climate of improved cooperation between us," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
